intent: run the application once and write the archive

title: stop the application with SIGTERM so the JVM writes the archive
why: The JVM writes the archive on its way out. This was checked on JDK 25.0.1 with a trivial application: after SIGTERM the process exits with code 143 and both the .aot and the .jsa archive exist, and the JVM removes its own temporary AOT config file. A long-running server never exits by itself, so the tool must ask it to stop.
alternative: Process.destroyForcibly. It is used only after the shutdown grace has passed, because a JVM that is killed abruptly writes no archive.

title: accept a run only if the exit code is right and a non-empty archive exists
why: Exit code 0, or 143 after our own SIGTERM, shows the application ended as planned. The archive check is separate because a JVM can exit 0 and write nothing. With AppCDS and -Xshare:off this happens: exit 0, a warning, no archive (PR 27).
alternative: Trust the exit code alone, or the archive alone. No record of either being considered.

title: delete the archive after any failed run, and before every run
why: A JVM that calls System.exit(3) still writes an archive. A stale file or the file from a failed run could be mistaken for good output by a later step. This was found while writing the tests (PR 27).
alternative: Leave the files in place for debugging. The full application log stays on disk for that purpose.

title: send application output to a log file and quote its last 40 lines on failure
why: Inferred from the code: the full output stays on disk, and a TrainingException carries the exit code and the last 40 lines so the cause is visible without opening the file. The PR does not give a further reason.

title: let a ReadyCondition decide when to stop the application
why: The runner must not know how a given framework signals that it has started. PR 27 describes ReadyCondition as the seam for the exit modes of issues 5 and 6; processExits and afterDelay exist as the first two.
alternative: Build one stop rule into the runner. Unknown whether it was considered.

title: allow 2 minutes after SIGTERM before treating the shutdown as failed
why: The AOT cache is assembled during JVM exit: the main process waits for a child process that writes the cache (seen in the JDK 25 test). On a large application this takes time (PR 27). The value is a default and can be set per run.

name: TrainingRunner
role: Starts the application with the recording flag, waits for the ReadyCondition, stops it with SIGTERM, then checks the exit code and the archive
conditions: Throws TrainingException on timeout, crash, no archive or a shutdown that exceeds the grace period; leaves no archive after a failure

name: TrainingSpec
role: Everything for one run: java binary, strategy, archive path, JVM and application arguments, environment, log file, timeout, shutdown grace, ready condition
conditions: Timeout and grace must be positive; the application arguments must say what to run, for example -jar app.jar

name: ReadyCondition
role: Decides when the application has started enough to be stopped; may wait for exit, wait a fixed time, or poll
conditions: Returns normally when the condition is met or the process has already exited; throws TimeoutException when it is not met in time

name: TrainingException
role: Failure of a training run, with the last log lines in the message and the log file path

subject: System.exit still writes an archive
why: A JVM that calls System.exit during training still dumps an archive on exit. The exit code check, not the archive check, rejects such a run, and the runner then deletes the file.

subject: POSIX only
why: Process.destroy sends SIGTERM on Linux and macOS. On Windows it kills the process, so no archive is written. Containers run Linux, so this is accepted and documented.

subject: AOT assembly happens at exit
why: With -XX:AOTCacheOutput the JVM records a temporary configuration file and then starts a child process to assemble the cache while the main process waits. Stopping the application early or killing it breaks this.

subject: AOT assembly happens at exit
why: With -XX:AOTCacheOutput the JVM records a temporary configuration file and then starts a child process to assemble the cache while the main process waits (seen in the JDK 25 test). The shutdown grace period must cover this time.
